811.event_title: Ferdinand Ward's firm ruins Ulysses S. Grant
811.event: After his presidency, Ulysses S. Grant became a partner in Grant & Ward, the Wall Street firm of his son Buck and the young financier Ferdinand Ward, whose apparent ability to produce large returns Grant admired, and the Grant family put most of its savings into it. Ward was secretly running what would now be called a Ponzi scheme, and in May 1884 the firm collapsed, leaving Grant nearly penniless and owing a $150,000 personal loan from William Vanderbilt. Ward was convicted of fraud and sent to Sing Sing prison, while Grant, already ill with cancer, wrote his Personal Memoirs to provide for his family.
811.explanation: Grant's warm trust in a charming partner of bad character grew year by year until it destroyed his fortune, and his memoirs were written in the shadow of that ruin.
811.tie_back: The kural says that when people of poor character seem to love you intensely, it is better for that friendship to shrink than to grow, and Grant's closeness to Ward grew until it consumed nearly everything he had.
811._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the cost of an attachment to a man of bad character, though Ward's relationship with Grant was a business partnership presented as admiration rather than a documented show of personal affection.

812.event_title: Marshal Marmont takes his corps over to the Allies
812.event: Auguste Marmont had first met Napoleon at Toulon, served as his aide-de-camp, sailed back with him from Egypt and rose under him to become a marshal and duke of Ragusa. In 1814, as the Allied armies closed in, Marmont capitulated at Paris on 30 March and on 5 April went over to the Allied side with his army corps, which had been guarding the road to Fontainebleau. Napoleon abdicated the next day, and under the restored Bourbon king Marmont was made a peer of France, while his title gave French the verb raguser, meaning to betray.
812.explanation: Marmont had shared in Napoleon's rise for twenty years, but when there was no more to be gained from him he left at the moment of greatest need.
812.tie_back: The kural describes those who befriend you while there is gain and leave when the gain is gone, and Marmont's change of sides came exactly when Napoleon's fortunes collapsed.
812._accuracy_note: A close fit to the kural's fair-weather friend, though Marmont's own reasons are debated and the sources describe his actions rather than his motives.

813.event_title: Bessus seizes Darius III and claims the Persian throne
813.event: After his defeat by Alexander the Great at Gaugamela, the Persian king Darius III retreated east, accompanied by Bessus, his relative and satrap of Bactria. In 330 BCE Bessus and other satraps arrested the king, and as Alexander's forces closed in, Darius was killed by his captors. Bessus then proclaimed himself king under the name Artaxerxes V, but within a year his own officers handed him over to Alexander, who had him executed.
813.explanation: A kinsman and trusted governor treated his fallen king as a prize to be used for his own advancement, and his gain lasted barely a year.
813.tie_back: The kural sets the friend who weighs up what he stands to get beside the thief, and Bessus weighed his king's misfortune as a chance to seize the crown for himself.
813._accuracy_note: A clear case of a close supporter acting for his own gain, though Bessus was a kinsman and subordinate rather than a personal friend, and the ancient sources differ on who struck the fatal blow.

814.event_title: Mir Jafar's cavalry stands aside at the Battle of Plassey
814.event: Before the battle, Robert Clive of the East India Company and the Jagat Seth bankers secretly promised Mir Jafar, one of the commanders of Siraj-ud-Daulah, nawab of Bengal, that he would become nawab if Siraj were defeated. At Plassey the nawab's army greatly outnumbered Clive's, but Mir Jafar, commanding a large body of the nawab's cavalry, kept his troops out of the fighting. Clive won, and Mir Jafar was installed as nawab, ruling largely as a puppet of the British.
814.explanation: Plassey was decided less by fighting than by a commander who abandoned his own side in the middle of the battle, and it opened the way to British rule in Bengal.
814.tie_back: The kural warns against companions who are like an untrained horse that throws its rider in the midst of battle, and Mir Jafar left his nawab exposed at the very moment of combat.
814._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's image of a companion who fails you on the battlefield itself.

815.event_title: Pompey is killed on arriving in Egypt
815.place: Off the coast of Egypt near Pelusium
815.event: After his defeat by Julius Caesar at Pharsalus, Pompey the Great sailed to Egypt, expecting help from the court of the young king Ptolemy XIII, whose father Ptolemy XII had been his ally and client. The king's advisers, including Pothinus and the general Achillas, feared offending the victorious Caesar. Pompey was killed in a small boat as he was brought ashore, before he could set foot in Egypt.
815.explanation: Pompey had supported the Ptolemaic house in its time of need, but when he came seeking protection, those he had helped gave him none.
815.tie_back: The kural says the friendship of small-minded people who will not protect you even after you have done everything for them is better never gained, and Pompey met his end at the hands of the court he had long supported.
815._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the friend who does not stand as protection, though the tie was a political alliance with a royal house rather than a personal friendship.

816.event_title: Charles I shields his favourite, the Duke of Buckingham
816.event: George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham, was the closest friend and chief minister of King Charles I, and he led England's war policy. A naval expedition against Cadiz in 1625 failed, and in 1626 the House of Commons blamed Buckingham and tried to impeach him, but Charles imprisoned one of the impeachment managers, Sir John Eliot, and dissolved Parliament rather than give up his favourite. Buckingham's landing on the Ile de Re in 1627 also ended in failure, and the king's quarrels with Parliament over money and his favourite deepened.
816.explanation: Charles's intimacy with an unsuccessful favourite cost him the cooperation of Parliament at the start of his reign, beginning the conflict that later led to civil war.
816.tie_back: The kural says that distance, or even enmity, with the wise is worth far more than close friendship with a fool, and Charles chose his favourite over the counsel of Parliament at great cost.
816._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of the cost of intimacy with an unwise favourite, though Buckingham was a capable courtier rather than a fool in every sense and Parliament was not simply a gathering of the wise.

817.event_title: Peter the Great rebuilds his army after defeat at Narva
817.event: In November 1700 Charles XII of Sweden routed Peter the Great's much larger Russian army at the Battle of Narva. In the following years Peter regrouped his troops and carried out sweeping military reforms, forming new regiments with modern weapons, uniforms and tactics, often with the help of foreign officers and engineers, and building up foundries and arms works. Russia retook Narva by siege in 1704 and decisively defeated Sweden at Poltava in 1709.
817.explanation: The harsh lesson of defeat by an enemy did more to make Russia a military power than years of comfortable court life had done.
817.tie_back: The kural says that what comes from enemies is worth far more than the friendship of those who only laugh along with you, and what Peter learned from the Swedes at Narva became the foundation of his later victories.
817._accuracy_note: Illustrates the value of what an enemy teaches, but the contrast with merely pleasant friends is the commentators' reading and is not shown directly by the event.

818.event_title: Bernadotte's corps takes part in neither Jena nor Auerstedt
818.event: On the day Napoleon defeated the Prussians at Jena, Marshal Davout's single corps fought and beat the main Prussian army at nearby Auerstedt. Marshal Bernadotte's I Corps, positioned between the two battlefields, took part in neither battle, despite requests from Davout for support. Napoleon blamed Bernadotte for failing to help, but did not bring him to a court-martial; historians still debate whether Bernadotte disobeyed or was following ambiguous orders.
818.explanation: A capable marshal's corps stood idle while a colleague fought against heavy odds, and Napoleon's trust in him was never the same, though he made no public break.
818.tie_back: The kural advises letting friendship quietly slacken, without announcement, with those who fail to do what they could easily have done, and Napoleon set aside formal punishment while his confidence in Bernadotte waned.
818._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Bernadotte's absence is certain, but whether he deliberately held back is disputed, and Napoleon's response was more anger withheld than a planned quiet withdrawal of friendship.

819.event_title: Pizarro takes Atahualpa's ransom and executes him
819.event: In November 1532 the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca. Atahualpa offered to fill a large room with gold, and twice over with silver, in exchange for his release, and over the following months his people delivered the treasure. In 1533, having received the ransom, Pizarro had Atahualpa tried on a series of charges and executed, and the treasure was melted down and shared among the Spaniards.
819.explanation: The ransom agreement showed how worthless Pizarro's undertakings were once he had what he wanted.
819.tie_back: The kural says that ties with people whose deeds are one thing and whose words another are painful even in a dream, and Atahualpa kept his side of the bargain only to find that Pizarro's deeds bore no relation to the terms agreed.
819._accuracy_note: A clear case of words and deeds at odds, but the relationship was captor and captive rather than friendship, so it illustrates the kural only partly.

820.event_title: Dickens portrays his friend Leigh Hunt as Harold Skimpole
820.event: Charles Dickens and the poet and essayist Leigh Hunt were friends of long standing. In Bleak House, published in monthly parts in 1852-53, Dickens created Harold Skimpole, a charming but irresponsible sponger, and readers who knew Hunt recognised him in the character. In a letter to John Forster in 1853 Dickens called Skimpole an exact portrait of a real man, the caricature caused Hunt much distress, and Dickens later apologised.
820.explanation: A friendship kept up in private was damaged when one friend held the other up to public ridicule in a widely read novel.
820.tie_back: The kural warns against coming close to those who are friendly at home but run you down in public, and Dickens's private friendship with Hunt sat beside a public caricature that all their acquaintances recognised.
820._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for private friendship joined to public mockery, though Dickens's portrait was fiction rather than open denunciation, and he did not intend it as an attack on Hunt's writing.
